About 1100–1200 mL of blood flows through the kidneys per minute, roughly one-fifth of cardiac output. GFR is about 125 mL/min.
GFR is the amount of filtrate formed by the kidneys per minute: about 125 mL/min, or about 180 L/day.
The JGA is formed by cellular modifications in the distal convoluted tubule and afferent arteriole. It helps regulate GFR.
Tubular epithelial cells in different nephron segments perform reabsorption by active or passive mechanisms.
Water and some solutes may be reabsorbed passively. Nitrogenous wastes are generally secreted or excreted, not mainly reabsorbed.

PCT reabsorbs the maximum amount: nearly all nutrients and about 70–80% of electrolytes and water. It also maintains ionic and pH balance by secreting H+ and ammonia and reabsorbing HCO3-.
Descending limb is permeable to water and helps maintain medullary osmolarity. Ascending limb is impermeable to water but permits transport of electrolytes.

The collecting duct extends from cortex to inner medulla, reabsorbs large amounts of water under ADH, helps form concentrated urine, and contributes to urea recycling.
The medullary osmotic gradient is mainly due to NaCl and urea.
Fluid loss stimulates the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary to release ADH, which increasereases water reabsorption in the later nephron segments and prevents diuresis.
ADH can also act as vasopressin, causing vasoconstriction and increasereasing blood pressure.

When GFR or blood pressure falls, juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which becomes angiotensin II, a powerful vasoconstrictor that helps raise blood pressure and GFR.
Angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which increasereases Na+ and water reabsorption from DCT and helps restore blood pressure and GFR.
ANF is released by atria when blood volume/pressure is high. It causes vasodilation and decreasereases blood pressure, acting as a check on the renin-angiotensin mechanism.
